doc.citation: Mehlqvist, K., Wigforss-Lange, J. & Vajda, V. 2015 (for 2014). A palynological study from Sweden reveals stable terrestrial environments during Late Silurian extreme marine conditions. Earth and Environmental Science Transactions of the Royal Society of Edinburgh 105, 149–158.
doc.comment: Twenty primary Klinta samples contain 159 positive table entries representing 26 spore taxa. Five additional entries capture explicitly named occurrences repeated from earlier studies; these are secondary reports and require deduplication against those papers. Primary taxon spellings follow Table I, including its apparent errors; Scylasapora is mapped to Scylaspora in genus. Primary illustrated flags mean the taxon is illustrated in Fig. 7; the caption does not identify the source sample. Klinta's Ludfordian age has independent marine biostratigraphic support. No reworking is reported.

items.setting_as_reported: near-shore tidally-influenced environment grading from open marine shallow subtidal to lagoonal intertidal conditions
items.notes: Uppermost analysed sample. Scylaspora klintaensis permits tentative correlation with its first appearance at 112 m in Klinta 1. The 14 m composite combines five stratigraphic sections; the succession comprises the Bjär and Bjärsjö members.

items.age_basis_detail: The age at this drillcore level is repeated from Mehlqvist et al. (2012); its independent dating evidence is not specified here.
items.notes: Secondary report of the first appearance datum of Scylaspora klintaensis from Mehlqvist, Vajda & Steemans (2012), Early land plant spore assemblages from the Late Silurian of Skåne, Sweden. Not a newly analysed sample in this paper.

items.age_basis_detail: Age repeated in the comparison with Hagström (1997) and Gray et al. (1974); dating evidence is not specified here.
items.setting_as_reported: nearshore, possibly deltaic, deposits
items.notes: Secondary comparison, principally from Hagström (1997), Land-derived palynomorphs from the Silurian of Gotland, Sweden; Gray et al. (1974) is also cited. Fourteen species are said to be shared with Klinta, but only six shared taxa are named, followed by three taxa present on Gotland and absent from Klinta. This is an incomplete species list, not new sampling. The wider Hagström material spans middle Llandovery to upper Ludlow.

items.locality: Rumney Inlier (south Wales) and Towy Anticline (southwest Wales)
items.age_basis_detail: Age repeated from Burgess & Richardson (1995); dating evidence is not specified here.
items.setting_as_reported: near-shore marine sediments
items.notes: Secondary comparison with Burgess & Richardson (1995), Late Wenlock to Early Přídolí cryptospores and miospores from south and southwest Wales, Great Britain. The Ludfordian subset contains 16 taxa: 11 trilete and five cryptospore taxa; trilete spores constitute 69%. The named shared taxa are not individually assigned to levels here, so the broader reported interval is retained. The paper discusses potentially earlier occurrence of Artemopyra brevicosta in Avalonia than Baltica.

items.formation: McAdam Brook and Moydart formations, Arisaig Group
items.age_basis_detail: Compared interval is described as dated to Ludlow and represented by the libycus–poecilomorphus Assemblage Zone; no independent dating evidence is specified here.
items.setting_as_reported: silisiclastic mudstone and siltstone deposits
items.notes: Secondary comparison with Beck & Strother (2001), Silurian spores and cryptospores from the Arisaig group, Nova Scotia, Canada. The selected interval contains 25 taxa; only ten shared species are explicitly listed here. Deposition is described as more distal, with a larger catchment than Klinta. The printed comma in A, dilutus is retained.

items.age_basis_detail: Age repeated from Wellman (1993); dating evidence is not specified here.
items.setting_as_reported: continental sediments
items.notes: Secondary comparison with Wellman (1993), A land plant microfossil assemblage of Mid Silurian age from the Stonehaven Group, Scotland. Cryptospores constitute c. 88% and trilete spores 8%. Ten species are said to be shared with Klinta, but several are identified only to genus in this comparison. Three additional species present in Scotland but absent from Klinta are named. Psedodyadospora is retained as printed.
